Any structure, like a plane structure for example, must in general be interpreted as a geomet- rical infinitely indeterminate structure. The Finite Element method is now used to convert this infinite system to a finite one, i.e. to discretizise it.
 A discrete solution, consisting of n unknowns, is computed instead of the continuous solution. For the static analysis these unknowns are for instance the displacements of particular points, the so-called nodes. These nodes are connected to each other by means of mechanically simplified members, the so-called elements. One can obtain the displacements of the entire region through interpolation of the nodal values inside the elements. The continuous plane structure is thus represented by a large - yet finite - number of elements.
 The power of Finite Elements lies in their universal applicability to any geometrical shape and almost any loading. This is achieved by the following building block principle. Individual ele- ments, which describe parts of the structure in a computer oriented manner, are assembled into a complete structure. Regular frame structures must be understood as a special case of this principle, in which a finite number of nodes leads to an exact solution.
 The task of SOFIMSHA is to export or import the total volume of nodes and elements with high effectiveness. Generating features are on a first glance left to the CADINP possibilities, however there are very mighty options available for the generation, copying and extrusion. Complex irregular structures should be defined via SOFIMSHC or SOFiPLUS.
 Exactly one database is available for each system, to which each module has unlimited access. A system is seen as the entirety of the parts forming a structure or a substructure, which co- operate statically during the systems life-span. During the design a partial system can be analysed separately.
 With a restart one may modify boundary conditions or add new nodes and elements. Elements may be changed, however nodes and especially used nodes are not allowed to have their coordinates changed.

The coordinate systems and the notations conform to DIN 1080.
 The nodal coordinates, displacements and rotations as well as loads and reaction forces are described in a global cartesian right-handed system X-Y-Z. The input can also be given in polar, cylindrical or spherical coordinates, which are however transformed automatically by the program to cartesian ones. Local coordinate systems, which are described in the next section, exist for the elements as well.
 The displacements and rotations are vectors with three components along the coordinate di- rections. These components are positive when they act in the positive coordinate axis direction. Rotational components are positive if they rotate clockwise about the given axis when looking into the positive direction of the axis. The same holds for forces and moments. For warping torsion we have a seventh scalar degree of freedom for the warping.
 If the observer is looking from the birds eye view he will believe to see a right or left handed 2D coordinate system depending on the orientation of the vertical axis . We use the designation of the ”first” and the ”second” horizontal axis in the counter clock wise orientation. It is advisable in some countries to define the global coordinate system such that the Z-axis coincides with the direction of gravity. In case of plane structures only the Y-X plane is considered. For axisymmetric analysis the X-axis is the axis of rotation.

Nodes are no elements in the general sense, they may be created automatically for any gen- eration of elements. There is geometric filtering avoiding to generate double nodes at a given position. If a special or multiple node numbers should be used at a selected position, it is therefore necessary to define that node before any generation takes place.
 A very important feature is a list of nodes, called a FIT within SOFIMSHA / SOFIMSHC. These lists are saved to the database and my be used as a singkle element, partly or in combination for other generations, loadings or boundary conditions. A FIT will be created for any generation of nodes along a line automatically, but it may be created also from existing nodes by a special selection. If that selection requires a combination of lists, the sequence is calculated on base of a minimum travelling path measured in number of nodes.

The truss or cable element can only carry one constant axial force. In case of a non-linear analysis, the cable element can not sustain any compression. For the local coordinate axis only the x-axis of the beam direction is available.

These elements are defined by two nodes and their straight connection, which is either the centrobaric axis or the origin of the sectional coordinate system. It is also the x-axis of the local coordinate system. The element in-between can either be prismatic or arbitrarily haunched with cross section jumps. Several elements may be combined with the same or a continuous number to a continuous beam element. In case of plane structures the direction of the z-axis is defined such that this is the main laoding direction, i.e. bending occurs only about the y- axis. In case of three-dimensional structures however, the orientation of the coordinate system should be specified explicitly.
 The cross section is defined with the program AQUA, in any parallely shifted y’-z’ coordinate system. Internal forces and moments of the beams are positive, when they act at the positive section in the positive direction.

The solid element of SOFiSTiK is a general six-sided element with eight nodes (BRIC), which can degenerate down to a tetrahedron. As a rule, a significantly improved accuracy is achieved through non-conforming formulations, so that the introduction of the 21-noded elements is not necessary.

The partitioning of a mesh is based on two requirements. On the one hand the mesh should be as fine as possible, so as to obtain the most accurate results. The factors opposing that are:
 - The computing times increase by n2, when the number of elements n are increased.
 - In case of very fine partitioning, round-off errors are amplified so that the solution may become unusable. As a rule of thumb, a logical partitioning of a free span consists of 5 up to 20 elements.
 - In construction practice it is not sensible to attempt to model and design all types of singularities. One should strive for a partitioning that is not too fine.

The Finite-Element system is a discrete system and it can thus only handle discrete loads. Every loading must therefore be converted to so-called nodal loads. A nodal load should not be confused with a point load. The difference is illustrated in the following figure
 A mesh refinement leads to new nodal loads in case of a uniform load (a and d), but not in case of point loads.
 On one hand, this means that a given mesh has a limited resolution for loadings. The coarser mesh (a, b, c) can not make the differentiation between two point loads and a uniform load upon the element grid or a point load at the middle of the element.
 It also means on the other hand, that a loading can be applied as a point load on a node only when its load induction area is smaller than the size of the adjacent elements. When inducing , for example, a point load upon a plate, each new mesh refinement in the area of the load will compute larger shear forces each time, due to the better modelling of the singularity. Therefore, one should either select an element size that will not be smaller than the plate thickness, or define the loads in the form of distributed loading with their actual contact surfaces.

To a large extent an exact description of the geometry is possible in the case of beam elements. A single beam element may be used from one support to the next. However, a typical FE partitioning of the geometry is necessary in the following cases:
 - Kinematic constraint with elastic foundation (Boundary element)
 - Dynamic analyses (nodal masses)
 - Buckled centrobaric axis (e.g. haunches)
 - Large deformations according to 3rd order theory
 The partitioning may only become so fine, that the lengths of the individual beams are approx- imately the same as their cross section dimensions. When their lengths become smaller than these dimensions, it is required that the correct shear deformation areas of the cross sections are defined. Artificially large stiffnesses must also be avoided, as well as the direct combination of elements with very different lengths.
 The results of the element can be obtained at all of its sections. Superpositioning and dimen- sioning can only take place at these sections.

For the simplest case the boundary conditions at the nodes are specified by suppressing the corresponding degrees of freedom. An elastic support is obtained by means of appropriate elements.
 There is however a frequent need for special support conditions, which the engineer would like to model using infinitely large stiffnesses. Due to numerical reasons the modelling should not be done with elements possessing very large stiffnesses, but with dependent degrees of freedom (kinematic constraints) instead. The need for such constraints arises e.g. for oblique supports or rigidly connected nodes. In general, every dependent degree of freedom can be expressed as a linear combination of other displacements or rotations:
 d = 1d1 + 2d2 + ...
 (2.6)
 These conditions are explicitly considered in the assembly of the global stiffness matrix and they are therefore numerically stable instead of any artificially rigid elements.
 These combinations can be directly formulated with the record KINE and they can be arbi- trarily convoluted. However, the memory requirements for solving a problem increase with the number of constraints and especially with the number of recursive associations.
 Coupling conditions have a distinct direction, they can be defined recursively up to 99 levels. Cyclic references or overlapping reference definitions are not possible however. When defining the boundary conditions multiple definitions will be combined in general based on a vector approach.
 Standard conditions are available for the most frequent cases of constraints in the record NODE and the node coupling conditions.
 In the node output dependent degrees of freedom are designated by a * or a negative equation number. All displacements are always output, and they comply to the specified dependencies. With ECHO REAC (program ASE, SEPP, TALPA ...) the support reactions can either be calcu- lated separately for each node or in pairs for coupled nodes; in the latter case they represent the forces transmitted through the kinematic constraint.
 Attention: Inappropriate use of kinematic constraints of the KINE type or the slave kinematic constraints (KPX through KPZ) may lead to mechanically absurd results (forces moved by kinematic constraints may violate the moment equilibrium).

A skewed support for a node can be always described by a single direction. The node is then either only supported in that direction (PR or MR) or it is supported in all directions transvers to that direction (PT or MT) . The latter case then allows a displacement only in that selected direction.

All couplings between distant nodes will generate rigid body contributions which are needed to fulfill the equilibrium of moments. The kinematic constraints KP, KL, KQ and KF describe rigid bodies to which the dependent nodes are connected through a hinge (KP), or through a connection with fixed rotation about one (KQ=KP+KMR), two (KL=KP+KMT) or all three (KF) directions. One single plane may be activated in special cases (KPEX, KPEY, KPEZ and KFEX, KFEY, KFEZ). This is for instance the case when defining a slab, which allows lateral bending but not in-plane distortion.

Symmetry conditions are a rarely needed special case of kinematic constraints. Whereby the respective symmetry or anti-symmetry conditions are assigned to the mid-perpendicular of the line connecting two nodes. In most cases the definition of a symmetry condition is more sensi- ble by means of an inclined support. The direction of the support must then be perpendicular to the symmetry plane. PRMT defines a symmetry and PTMR an anti-symmetry.

Eccentric connections, e.g. between a beam and a plate, can be specified with KF. Beam elements may have explicit excentricities or implicit by the definition of the sectional coordinate system. For shell elements the mid surface or the upper or lower side may be positioned in the plane of the nodes.

A special class of kinematic constraints imposes the same displacements or rotations to several nodes (KPX to KMT). Their application is useful e.g. in the description of rigid foundation plates, which are not allowed to rotate. These kinematic constraints act upon particular degrees of freedom and are thus more flexible. The danger on the other hand is that their inappropriate use can produce undesired offset moments.

The formulation of the boundary conditions of plate elements is not uncritical. Especially the Mindlin-element has some peculiarities which should be considered.
 According to Kirchhoff’s theory two internal forces exist at an edge, namely the bending mo- ment and the equivalent shear force. The latter consists of the shear force and the torsional moment, and that is why both can have values along a free edge different from zero. By contrast, Mindlin’s theory recognises three support conditions for the three internal forces i.e. bending moment, torsional moment and shear force. A support for the torsional moment would for example suppress the rotations perpendicular to the edge.
 Free edges do not have constraints of any type. The reaction forces along such edges are, within the bounds of computing accuracy, zero. However the internal forces inside the elements are not always exactly zero, due to the numerical method.
 Perfectly fixed edges can be input without any problems. For the interpretation of the results
 however, it is important to know that the torsional reaction moments must be taken up. This takes place automatically in the output of the BOUN-elements, whereby these are converted to corresponding support loadings.
 Here one has a choice between the so-called soft support (only PZ) and the hard support (PZ+MT). In case of the soft support, shear deformations are still allowed along the edge, and thus a shear force too; in some cases this can lead to considerable deviations from Kirchhoff’s plate theory. On the other hand is the soft support more suitable for the manipulation of uplifting corners as well as of re-entrant corners. Particularly in the case of obtuse corners, the hard support leads to an undesired fixation.
 There are generally four ways to describe such supports:
 • Point- or line-support
 This type of support is mainly used for thin supports (width < plate thickness). The size of the adjacent elements should be selected in such a way that their gravity centre lies on the round section which is critical for the punch-through check. The dimensioning of the shear force takes place inside the element; for the moment, on the safe side, in the nodes of the support.

This type of support is mainly used for thin supports (width < plate thickness). The size of the adjacent elements should be selected in such a way that their gravity centre lies on the round section which is critical for the punch-through check. The dimensioning of the shear force takes place inside the element; for the moment, on the safe side, in the nodes of the support..
 • Pivoting column head support
 The column is described by a node having a fixed support and a possible rotational spring stiffness, this node is usually is not an element node. The column area is described by means of a single element as well as coupling conditions between the four element nodes and the column node, which specifies that the cross section will remain plane without a restraint of the moment (KP for columns, KQ for walls). The size of the element can be between 2/3 of the column area (e.g. for circular columns) and the actual column area (e.g. for rectangular column cross section). The size also depends on where one wants to arrange the resultant of the bearing stress.
 The central element has a zero shear force and thus a uniform moment corresponding to the moment of the section along the face of the column. One should arrange additional elements for the shear force check, whereby their gravity centre lies on the round section used for that check , or directly carry out a punch-through check.
 • Elastic foundation
 This option is ideal for elastic supports of large areas, for which a rounded moment above the support is desired. Large Winkler coefficients however, result in undesired restraints. The selection of the Winkler coefficient is thus critical, and this option should only be applied to minor foundations.
 • Special conditions
 In principle any arbitrary conditions can be formulated through kinematic constraints. The effect though must be checked in every case.

The modelling of joists in plate structures presents a special problem. Besides the option of modelling them with folded structure elements or solid elements, which are ruled out for
 practical processing, one has a choice between two other options:
 • The joist is modelled as an eccentric beam connected to a plane shell (plate- and disk action). The area of the joist and its moment of inertia are determined from the protruding part of the joist.
 For the dimensioning the results of the shell and the beam should be combined into the total internal forces and moments for a T-beam.
 This is a general method and always correct. It captures the effective widths and their distribution in the system.
 • The joist is modelled as an additional element to a plate, by defining all its cross sectional values (area, moment of inertia) as follows:
 Additional values = Total values of T-beam effective
 - contributions of the plate to the effective width
 The total stiffness is correctly modelled in this manner. When dimensioning joists with small heights one should always make constructive decisions, e.g. assembling the individual values and applying them to a T-beam cross section.

The program SOFiMSHA generates the basic structural system for plane or three-dimensional structures. On one hand the system consists of the nodes, defined by a number, their coordi- nates and geometric support conditions. On the other hand there are the elements, which are connected to each other at these nodes.
 For a restart of the system element properties or boundary conditions may be changed, ele- ments may be deleted or added. Only the coordinates of any existing node may not be changed any more. The orientation of the gravity, the group divisor or any defined base number of a group may not be changed either. Thus all elements added to existing groups must fit in the assigned space of numbers.
 SOFiMSHA has a more element based input mode than its predecessor GENF. Nodes will be generated mostly automatically. Nearly all elements have a mesh generation option. The basic concept is either a regular subdivision or a non-regular nodal sequence called a FIT. For more details see NODE.
 Cross sections and materials have to be defined beforehand with the program AQUA.

Nodes are assigned with a number for identification. For generation facilities new nodes will be automatically introduced or existing nodes identified with an effective octree search. Node numbers need not be in a consecutive order. The maximum value of these numbers is limited to 999999, due to the output format. The node numbering has normally no influence on the band width of the system of equations, because subsequent to the system’s generation an optimisation of the profile takes place. Undefined nodes do not have any influence.
 With nearly all element definitions it is possible to insert intermediate nodes automatically. This has either to be defined with the number of subdivision segments and an optional mid node, or a already defined sequence of nodes (FIT) may be used. In both cases new nodes will be compared against already existing ones and created only if necessary.

Elements are also identified by an arbitrary number within the selected element group. If the number is not specified, the element number is automatically assigned. Although an element number may only be used once for each element type. Elements can only be defined once.
 The element number contains the group number. The latter is for example the integer part of the element number divided by a freely defined divisor. The default value of this divisor GDIV of the record SYST is 0, i.e. all elements are assigned to group 0. If the elements are subdivided into groups with a different value for GDIV, any elements of the group 0 that follow a group initiation with the record GRP are assigned to that group by their element number, i.e. the program changes the element numbers so that they fit into the active group.
 Groups can be used to select a particular structural system or to define partial regions for post- processing or graphical representation. A sensible partitioning of a structure into such groups can be very helpful when evaluating the internal forces and moments at nodes. In case of
 folded structures, one should arrange the elements of each disk into separate groups.
 It is advantageous to number the elements in such a way, so that one can make use of the generation options during the system selection (groups) and the loading input (refer to STAR2, beam groups).
 The theoretical principals of the elements are described in the calculation programs.

The created structure is stored in the database (project file) and it can be represented graph- ically by the program WinGRAF; this can even be done for faulty systems, as long as the pro- gram has not terminated prematurely. Further processing of the analysis with other programs is only possible when the structure is free of errors.
 When no errors are detected, a profile optimisation is performed on the stiffness matrix, in order to minimise the cost of solving the system of equations for the structure.

At any time boundary conditions can be modified or new elements may be added with a Restart. However, existing elements and nodal coordinates remain unchanged. A restart takes place with the explicit input SYST REST. The following can be included in a Restart input:
 - Change support conditions and constraints for existing nodes
 - Add New nodes and new elements
 - Change element properties
 - Delete Elements

As SOFIMSHA follows a completely new and much more powerful concept for the generation of data, we have the situation that simple input data may be converted easily, but that depending on the complexity of the definition a rather expensive redefinition might be necessary which is beyond the scope of any automatic conversion. In many cases the input with an old GENF- version and the following export with AQUA/SOFIMSHA might be the most economically way to do the transition.
 Here following steps should be de noted or done:
 • Add the now mandatory group divisor in record SYST
 • Move all material and sectional definitions to AQUA
 Insert the item FIX for nodes of a planar system (there was no Z in GENF).
 •
 • Change of a few item names (e.g. KR instead of NR for BEAM)
 • Sections for haunched beams have now to be defined as a single string in the form 10.11. There are some minor restrictions of this format for generations.
 • Hinges of beams are defined with the beam itself. Beam sections are only defined with SECT.
 For other cases the following hints might be helpful:
 • Polar or spherical coordinates are defined with new special items. There is no longer the negative node number available for this effect.
 • Generation of bodes along a line is dound with NODE instead of BOUN or MESH. MESH and CUBE have been integrated as QUAD MESH/IMSH and BRIC MESH/IMSH. IMES has to be described with a QUAD FIT/IFIT now.
 • ALIN and SECT have been integrated in the record NODE. ALIN 101 100 102 0.5 becomes now NODE 101 0.5 NR1 100 102 "SS", and SECT 100 101 102 103 104 becomes NODE 100 NR1 101 102 103 104.
 • All implicit element generators (ENO/DNO/KNO) have to be replaced either with CADINP loops or by MESH or FIT Options.

The table defines **GRP**, the grouping mechanism used in **SOFiSTiK** to organize model elements. It distinguishes between two kinds of group identifiers: **primary groups** and **secondary groups**. Primary groups are addressed by an **integer group number** ranging from **1 to 999**. Secondary groups are identified by a **string composed of up to four text literals** (denoted as *Text Lit*4*). Additionally, an optional **reference number** can be provided to identify elements that belong to, or are located on, the same geometry. In typical workflows this reference value is **automatically set by the mesh generator**.

The table lists the configurable input fields (“Item” / “Description” columns) that define a group entry. The “Unit” column indicates expected data type/format, while “Default” specifies the preselected value when not explicitly provided.

### Fields described in the table
- **NO — “Group number or identifier”**  
  Specifies the primary group number or the secondary identifier text.  
  - **Unit / format:** `–/LIT` (i.e., numeric or literal-based input)  
  - **Default:** `!` (mandatory/required field; the table marks it as not optional)

- **REF — “Span, reference or sequence number”**  
  Used to further qualify the grouping, e.g., selecting a specific span/geometry location or ordering sequence.  
  - **Unit / format:** `–`  
  - **Default:** `0`

- **BASE — “Base number for this group”**  
  Provides a base numbering value associated with the group, enabling consistent numbering schemes across grouped entities.  
  - **Unit / format:** `–`  
  - **Default:** `*` (placeholder indicating derived or automatically determined base behavior)

- **ICS — “Construction stage number of activation”**  
  Indicates the construction stage at which the group becomes active (activated).  
  - **Unit / format:** `–`  
  - **Default:** `-` (no activation stage specified / not defined)

- **ICE — “Construction stage number of deactivation”**  
  Indicates the construction stage at which the group is deactivated (removed from active behavior).  
  - **Unit / format:** `–`  
  - **Default:** `-` (no deactivation stage specified / not defined)

- **TITL — “Title of the group”**  
  Human-readable label for the group.  
  - **Unit / format:** `Lit32` (text up to 32 characters)  
  - **Default:** `–` (no title by default)

### Overall meaning
This configuration table is essentially a **schema for defining group membership and lifecycle** (activation/deactivation via construction stages). It supports flexible identification (numeric primary vs. literal secondary), optional geometry/span referencing, and organizational metadata through a group title. It also relates to other element organization concepts referenced in the prompt (e.g., SYST, BEAM, QUAD, BRIC, SPRI, TRUS, CABL), suggesting that GRP is a cross-cutting mechanism used by multiple element types.

See also: SYST, BEAM, QUAD, BRIC, SPRI, TRUS, CABL

### Overall meaning of the table
This table serves as a quick reference showing that the **primary group number** is not intrinsic to the element number alone; it depends on the configured **group divisor**. The same element number (**3569**) produces different group numbers (**3**, **1**, **713**) under different GDIV values. This aligns with the surrounding specification: group number derivation is uniquely determined from the element number with two possible behaviors depending on SYST GDIV and the existence/state of GRP definitions; if no group records exist, the primary group is derived directly from the element number, otherwise element numbers are adjusted to fit the specified group constraints.

The table describes how **primary group numbers** and **element numbers** are determined and bounded, including the role of group “base” values and special-case behavior.

## Columns
- **Group**: The primary group identifier.
- **Base**: The base number assigned to the group (used as the origin for element numbering and/or validation).
- **Element number**: The allowable numeric range of element numbers that belong to that group.

## Semantics and relationships
1. **Primary group derivation (when no GRP definition is active)**  
   The primary group number (from **1 to 999**) is derived uniquely from the element number. The derivation depends on **SYST GDIV**:  
   - The group number is computed as the integer result of dividing the **element number by the group divisor** (GDIV).  
   - Example behavior is referenced to show “derived” grouping versus “configured/forced” grouping.

2. **Group base assignment and ordering**  
   - “All groups must be assigned an individual base number in increasing order.”  
   - An element number interval maps to group membership. That is, each group’s base defines the start of its interval (with explicit warnings about boundary behavior).

3. **Boundary and special constraints**
   - If **no base has been selected**, the **first element defined within a group** sets the base value.  
   - Element numbers **equal to the base number should be avoided**, but they are stated to be **still allowed when GDIV = 0**.
   - For **GDIV > 0**, bases for groups > 0 are **defined after generation**, becoming **multiples of GDIV**. As a consequence, continuous numbering patterns may no longer be possible (since element numbers are not constructed from base directly in the same way).

4. **Group 0 warning**
   - **Primary group 0** has special historical context and should **not** be used for deactivation in construction sequences.  
   - Additionally, **kinematic constraints without a group number may not be deactivated**.  
   - The table’s example includes Group 0 (none) with base 0, but the narrative warns it has special meaning.

5. **Rules for specified element numbers**
   - If a given element number is **not specified or is 0**, the system selects the **next free number in the current group**.
   - If the first element number is **above the group base**, element numbers are treated mostly as final and only corrected if they violate group limits.
   - Otherwise, if the provided number is not larger than **999,999**, it is added to the base for the final effective element number.
   - If a GRP record exists (or is re-established), element numbers may be **adjusted to fit within the specified primary group**; otherwise, the group is derived from the element number.

6. **Maximum limits**
   - **Maximum group number is 999** (for both derived and configured cases).
   - The **current limit for elements within a group** is **1,000,000**.
   - The maximum element number discussed (for printing/assignment behavior) is constrained such that “large element numbers may be given as an offset to the base number for printing.”

Overall, the table (with its accompanying text) defines a deterministic scheme: each group has a base and an element interval; element numbers either derive the group (when no GRP configuration is active) or are adjusted/constructed to comply with the configured group bases and limits.

The input table defines the **NODE** data structure used in a mechanical/finite-element context to specify **points of mechanical connection** between elements. Each node is identified by a **unique node number** (“NO”), which does not need to be consecutive. The table also supports setting node geometry (coordinates) and node-related constraints/boundary information. A key behavioral note (from the accompanying context) is that **the last provided input for a node is valid at any time**, and with a **RESTART** capability, nodes or boundary conditions may be added/changed. Additionally, during **mesh generation**, intermediate nodes may be created automatically; however, if a user needs a **special node with a fixed number at a particular location**, it must be defined explicitly before mesh generation.

The table columns are: **Item** (field name), **Description** (meaning and grouping), **Unit** (engineering unit or type), and **Default** (typical default values or “*” indicates no fixed default / value must be provided depending on use).

Key fields:

- **NO (Node number)**: Identifies the node. Type is unitless (“-/”). Default is marked as “!” indicating it is required.
- **X, Y, Z (Coordinates)**: Spatial coordinates of the node in meters:  
  - **X**: [m]1001, default **0**  
  - **Y**: [m]1001, default **0**  
  - **Z**: [m]1001, default **0**  
  The context implies these can be defined multiple times for the same node as long as no elements have been defined yet; later entries override earlier ones for that node.
- **FIX (Node constraints)**: Defines constraints at the node (likely fixed DOFs or related constraint flags). Unit is “Lit16” and default is “*” (not a single fixed default; depends on constraint specification).
- **NR1–NR4 (Reference node numbers)**: Up to four reference nodes can be provided for constraint definitions or coordinate relations (unitless, default “-”). These typically support kinematic relations (e.g., multi-point constraints) and/or polar-related constraints.
- **DX, DY, DZ (Directions)**: Direction vectors for kinematic constraints or polar boundary conditions in meters units with “1001” scaling: default “*” (direction magnitude/components must be meaningful for the intended constraint/boundary behavior).
- **PHIX, PHIY, PHIZ (Rotation angles)**: Rotation angles used for polar or spherical coordinate definitions. Units are degrees (or dimensionless angle) indicated as “[°]5”. Defaults are **0.0**.
- **PHIG (Inclination for spherical coordinates)**: Additional inclination angle for spherical coordinates. Units “[°]5”, default **0.0**.
- **DIV (Subdivision for MESH/IMSH)**: Mesh subdivision parameter (unitless). Default is “-”.
- **PROG (Progression of subdivision)**: Controls grading/progression of the subdivision (unitless). Default **1.0** (uniform progression).
- **SLN (Projection on structural line/axis, GAX)**: Defines projection onto a structural line or axis (via GAX). Unit shown as “-/Lit4”; default “-” (no fixed value unless the feature is used).
- **SAR (Projection on structural area/area, GAR)**: Defines projection onto a structural area (via GAR). Same unit/type pattern as SLN: “-/Lit4”; default “-”.
- **RC, XC, YC, ZC, DXC, DYC, DZC**: Parameters for cylindrical/spherical geometrical definitions:
  - **RC**: Radius of a sphere/cylinder, [m]1001, default “-” (typically required when using spherical/cylindrical projection or constraints)
  - **XC, YC, ZC**: Center coordinates of the sphere / point on axis of cylinder, each in [m]1001, default **0.0**
  - **DXC, DYC, DZC**: Direction components of the cylinder axis, unitless (“-” in table), defaults **0.0**
  
Overall, this table is a comprehensive schema for defining node identity, position, and a variety of constraint/projection/coordinate-system parameters (including kinematic constraint directions, polar/spherical angle settings, and cylinder/sphere geometry parameters). It is intended to be used before or alongside mesh generation, with special attention to the “last input wins” behavior and explicit node definition when fixed node numbering is required.

See also: SYST, TRAN, KINE

Nodes may be generated with the following possibilities:
 • Definition of literal MESH at position NO for a generation with automatic node numbers not yet used. All generated nodes are compared against already existent nodes and created only if necessary (see CTRL FIT).
 • Definition of literal IMSH at position NO for a generation with interpolated node numbers. All nodes already defined within the selected sequence are retained, the interpolation will be in between those nodes only.
 In both cases the following positions X and Y are used to specify two node numbers NA and NE. The number of subdivisions may be specified with DIV either as integer value n or as real factor 1/N. For IMSH it is also possible to specify at position Z an increment:
 NODE IMSH 101 181 10
 generates 111,121 .. 171
 NODE IMSH 101 181 DIV 8 dito NODE IMSH 101 181 DIV 1/8 dito
 At position Z a third node NM may be specified for MESH to define curved edges:
 •
 a positive number NM generates quadratic interpolated nodes based on the geometry de- fined by the three nodes NA, NM, NE. Node NM does not need to coincide with one of the final generated nodes.
 • a negative value NM generates circular interpolated nodes based on the geometry defined by the three nodes NA, NM, NE. Node NM does not need to coincide with one of the final generated nodes.
 With PROG one can define edges with a subdivision as geometric progressions. Starting at NA, each segment is PROG times the previous one. If PROG is negative, a symmetric partitioning takes place (length of the first segment equal to that of the last one).
 For the reference nodes it is possible to specify starting at item NR1 the definitions FIT k1 k2 or MESH/IMSH k1 k2 km. The divisions have to match of course.

Any Generation of nodes according to the preceding paragraph will save the list of generated node numbers to be reused for other generations. However it is also possible to generate a sequence of existing node numbers. Thus we have the following possibilities:
 •
 a literal FIT for NO will search for an already defined nodal sequence between start and end node. If a node sequence is found with a geometric length not longer than a certain threshold value of the direct connection (CTRL FIT) this will be used and DIV will be set to the subdivision found.
 • a literal FITL will search for all nodes which are located within the tolerance specified with CTRL GTOL on the straight line between start and end node, sort them according to their relative distance and create a FIT from that, thus also defining the default value of DIV.
 Again in both cases the following positions X and Y are used to specify two node numbers NA and NE.
 For the generation of elements, it is also possible to generate nodes or nodal fits onn the fly automatically. This has to be defined with the number of subdivision segments DIV or M and N for QUAD or M and N and K for BRIC and optional mid nodes NMi.

 In mesh refinements of plates and shells there is a problem in coupling the translational and rotational degrees of freedom. Very poor elements function with a plain interpolation. Due to the peculiarities exhibited by the formulation of the SEPP/ASE-elements, even in its simplest form, the INTE-conditions must be accordingly complicated. In case of regular elements by Kirchhoff’s theory for example, a cubic interpolation of the displacements and two of the rota- tions must be employed. Mindlin elements also work with the so-called Kirchhoff constraints. In principle of course, translations and rotations are interpolated independently of one another, yet proper additional conditions are used to make sure that the shear force corresponds to the derivative of the moment.
 A quadratic distribution of the bending deflection along with a linear distribution of the rotations can be accomplished through the introduction of an additional translational degree of freedom at the middle of an element’s side. This additional degree of freedom can be later eliminated. This method is also employed by V-couplings. Although the formulation is consistent and leads to considerably better results than the older methods, it is not recommended unlimited. In particular, it should not be used with non-conforming elements.
 The application of INTE in the direct vicinity of singularities is generally not recommended.

This table defines the data structure for an **EDGE** record, which is used to specify **edges as sequences of node IDs** for later **generations and for applying boundary conditions/loading**. In the database, the edge information is stored **only as a list of nodes along that edge**—no additional geometric or behavioral edge properties are contained in this record.

### Overall purpose
- Create an edge definition by listing the **node numbers** that belong to the edge.
- Support multiple edge records with the **same edge number** to extend or segment the node list.
- Allow special **literal identifiers** for edges, mainly intended for **boundary conditions and loading** (i.e., instead of numeric edge numbers).
- Interoperates with generators such as **SOFIMSHC / SOFiPLUS**, which automatically generate an EDGE with the **same number as each structural line** used for mesh generation.

### Fields and their meaning
1. **NO (Edge number or identifier)**  
   - Type: `—/Lit4`  
   - Meaning: Either a **numeric edge number** or a **literal identifier**.
   - Default shown: `!` (indicates a required/non-empty setting in the source specification).
   - This value is the key to grouping multiple records: **more than one record may share the same NO**.

2. **TYPE (Selection type of intermediate nodes)**  
   - Unit: `LIT`  
   - Default: `-` (unspecified/normal behavior)
   - Allowed values: **`NONE / FIT / FITL`**
   - Meaning: Controls how **intermediate nodes** between the explicitly listed node numbers are interpreted or selected.
     - `NONE`: no intermediate selection beyond explicitly provided nodes.
     - `FIT` / `FITL`: apply selection rules (commonly meaning “fit” or “interpolate/expand” intermediate nodes between given endpoints; the exact node-selection algorithm is defined elsewhere in the overall system specification).

3. **N1, N2, N3, …, N36 (Node numbers)**  
   - Type/unit: `—`  
   - Default: `-` (not set)
   - Meaning: Up to **36 node entries** (`N1` through `N36`) that together form the **ordered node list** along the edge.
   - These entries are the actual payload stored for the edge: the system uses them to define which mesh nodes belong to the edge.

### Node list range input feature (important for N1…N36)
To simplify regular numbering, the input can encode sequences using a **range notation that includes a negative element**. Example given:
- `101 -191` selects all defined nodes within the interval:

The table documents the input parameter structure for a kinematic constraint record (mentioned in the surrounding context alongside “See also: NODE” and “KINE”). This record defines *dependent* degrees of freedom (DOFs) at a node using a linear combination of *reference* DOFs from one or multiple other nodes. In general form, the dependent DOF is expressed as:

**(ND) = (ND1) · FD1 + … + (ND21) · FD21**

where **ND** is selected by combining a node number and a support-condition literal (**FIX**) that may include one or several DOFs. The reference DOFs are defined using node numbers plus a local DOF encoding **(node + 0.1 · local DOF)**.

The table is organized as an item list with columns **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. The entries are:

- **ND (Dependant node number)**  
  - **Type/Meaning:** identifies the dependent node for which the kinematic relation is created.  
  - **Unit:** “–” (no physical unit; it is an identifier).  
  - **Default:** marked with **“!”**, indicating a required field.

- **FIX (Dependent degrees of freedom)**  
  - **Type/Meaning:** specifies which DOFs at the dependent node are constrained, using a literal that can represent multiple DOFs.  
  - **Unit:** “Lit16” (enumerated literal).  
  - **Default:** also **“!”** (required).

- **ND1 … ND21 (Reference degree of freedom i)**  
  - **Type/Meaning:** for each reference term in the linear combination, **NDk** supplies the reference node plus the local DOF selection encoded as **node number + 0.1 · local DOF**.  
  - **Local DOF mapping (from context):**  
    - 1 = u, 2 = uy, 3 = uz  
    - 4 = φ (rotation), 5 = φy, 6 = φz, 7 = φb  
    - 0 = “same or corresponding DOF as FIX”  
  - **Units:** “LIT” (literal/identifier encoding).  
  - **Defaults:** “-” (no default; typically must be provided as needed for the selected relation order).

- **FD1 … FD21 (Factor for reference DOF i)**  
  - **Type/Meaning:** scalar coefficients multiplying each corresponding reference DOF term **NDk** in the linear combination.  
  - **Unit:** “–” (dimensionless).  
  - **Default:** “-”; however the context notes that **weights/functions default to 1.0** in general when not otherwise specified (implying typical FD values can default in some cases, depending on record semantics).

Overall, the table defines a flexible “up to 21-term” expansion: the user supplies one dependent node (**ND**) and dependent DOF set (**FIX**), then provides a list of reference DOFs (**ND1..ND21**) and their coefficients (**FD1..FD21**) to express how the dependent motion is kinematically constructed from reference motions. This supports cases such as weighted averaging of node motions (e.g., hanging nodes) or more specialized constraint generation, as described in the surrounding text.

This table defines the input fields of a “coordinate search” style CADINP variable record used to locate existing model entities (nodes or element points) based on spatial coordinates, with results stored into a named CADINP variable array. It is conceptually used for resolving generated entities after all input has been read (coordinates become available only later), and it supports special cases such as restarting with **SYST REST** when necessary.

### Columns
- **Item**: Field identifier/name in the record.
- **Description**: Meaning and expected content.
- **Unit**: Units for numeric entries (or “-” if not applicable).
- **Default**: Default values if not provided.

### Fields
1. **X**  
   - **Description**: Target x-coordinate used for the search.  
   - **Unit**: `[m]1001`  
   - **Default**: `0.0`

2. **Y**  
   - **Description**: Target y-coordinate used for the search.  
   - **Unit**: `[m]1001`  
   - **Default**: `0.0`

3. **Z**  
   - **Description**: Target z-coordinate used for the search.  
   - **Unit**: `[m]1001`  
   - **Default**: `0.0`

4. **VAR**  
   - **Description**: Name of a CADINP variable where the result(s) are written. The value is an array-like variable name; the leading `#` character is *not* included in the input.  
   - **Unit**: `Lit8` (as specified)  
   - **Default**: `!` (unspecified/mandatory in practice)

5. **IND**  
   - **Description**: Base index of the CADINP variable array to start writing results (index offset).  
   - **Unit**: `-`  
   - **Default**: `-`

6. **TOL**  
   - **Description**: Search tolerance radius (in meters) around (X,Y,Z).  
   - **Unit**: `[m]1001`  
   - **Default**: `*`  
   - **Behavior nuance**: If **TOL is negative**, only the closest matching node number is stored; otherwise all nodes within tolerance may be stored.

7. **TYP**  
   - **Description**: Object type to search for. Controls what entity IDs are collected and how. Options:
     - **NODE**: nodes
     - **QUAD**: QUAD elements
     - **BRIC**: BRIC elements  
   - **Unit**: `-`  
   - **Default**: `NODE`

8. **GRP**  
   - **Description**: Primary group number used mainly when **QUAD/BRIC elements overlap**. It selects the “first/primary” element among candidates when multiple elements contain the point.  
   - **Unit**: `-`  
   - **Default**: `-`

### Output semantics (from context)
- For **TYP = NODE**: the record saves the list of node numbers found within tolerance around the coordinate into the specified CADINP variable array.
- For **TYP = QUAD or BRIC**: it selects the first element whose volume contains the point (x,y,z). It then uses the element’s interpolation context: it records the involved **four/eight node numbers** and their **shape-function values** for those nodes (so downstream code can interpolate using the stored weights).
- Coordinate values of nodes can generally be obtained via special CADINP variables like:
  - `#COOR_X(nummer)`, `#COOR_Y(nummer)`, `#COOR_Z(nummer)`.

This coordinate search table is complementary: it supports resolving which nodes/elements correspond to geometric coordinates so that kinematic definitions can reference the correct entity IDs and interpolation weights.

The table describes the input syntax and meaning of fields for the **TRUS** (truss) element record. It is presented with columns **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**, where each *Item* corresponds to a keyword or parameter used in the TRUS command line. The defaults indicate the assumed behavior if a parameter is omitted. Overall, the record is used to define a truss member (or options for how it is generated) between two structural nodes and to specify mechanical properties and contact/nonlinear activation parameters.

### Main element definition items
- **NO** (*Number of truss member or option*; unit: “–”; default: `*`): Identifies the truss member number via `NO` or selects an option for how the record is interpreted. The description lists supported options under this item:
  - **PROP**: defines default values for subsequent TRUS records (also useful for imports; e.g., `TRUS PROP NCS 1` sets cross-section number for all following TRUS records).
  - **MESH**: generation of nodes.
  - **IMSH**: generation of nodes (likely import-mesh specific).
  - **FIT**: fit in existing nodes.
  - **FITL**: linear fit in existing nodes.
  The default `*` implies that NO is mandatory or context-dependent (since it can represent both an element number and a mode).

- **NA** (*Start node*; unit: “–”; default: `!`): Node index at one end of the truss element. The default `!` suggests it must be explicitly provided.

- **NE** (*End node*; unit: “–”; default: `!`): Node index at the other end of the truss element.

- **NCS** (*Cross section number*; unit: “–”; default: `1.`): References a truss cross-section definition. If not specified, cross-section number defaults to **1**.

- **PRE** (*Prestress force*; unit: `[kN]101`; default: `0.`): Prestressing force applied to the truss. Context notes indicate prestress is active in **all load cases**, so it generally cannot be used for load superposition with certain program features (e.g., MAXIMA) unless modeled as a separate load.

- **GAP** (*gap of contact*; unit: `[m]1001`; default: `0.`): Contact gap parameter used for models where separation/contact conditions are introduced; defaults to **0** (no gap).

- **CRAC** (*Tensile rupture force*; unit: `[kN]101`; default: `-`): Parameter controlling rupture in tension. Default `-` indicates not active/unspecified.

- **YIEL** (*Yield force (tension and compression)*; unit: `[kN]101`; default: `-`): Yield threshold applied for both tension and compression. Default `-` means yield behavior is not defined/used.

### Subdivision items (mesh refinement along the member)
- **DIV** (*Subdivision in Elements*; unit: “–”; default: `-`): Controls how the truss member is subdivided into multiple elements, enabling finer discretization along its length.

- **NM** (*optional 3rd subdivision node*; unit: “–”; default: `-`): Defines an additional subdivision/control node. The table notes “see comments in record NODE,” implying that NM interacts with node-related options and geometry handling.

### Additional contextual constraints (relevant for interpretation)
The provided context emphasizes modeling limitations and nonlinear activation:
- A truss element sustains **only tensile or compressive forces**; it **cannot** be processed with **SYST GIRD/SLAB**.
- Parameters like **GAP**, **CRAC**, and **YIEL** are stated to become effective **only within a non-linear analysis**, and the user must verify whether the chosen analysis program version supports this feature.

This record therefore combines (1) geometry definition via start/end nodes, (2) property assignment via cross-section and prestress, (3) optional nonlinear/contact rupture/yield parameters, and (4) optional discretization refinement via DIV/NM.

The table defines the input record **CABL** for **cable elements** in ASE, listing each parameter (“Item”) with a short meaning, its **Unit**, and a **Default** value. It also documents options for how cable element nodes are generated or linked.

**Overall record logic:** A single CABL entry can either (a) create one or multiple cable elements based on node generation options, or (b) assign properties for subsequent CABL records using **PROP**. The table is structured into (1) main element definition items and (2) optional subdivision parameters.

### Main items (element definition)

- **NO** (unit: “–”, default: “!”)  
  Represents either the **number of the cable element** or an **option keyword**. The table indicates special keywords:
  - **PROP**: “Definition of default values” that will apply to later CABL records (important for imports and successive element definitions).
  - **MESH** / **IMSH**: “Generation of nodes” (two different mesh-based node generation variants).
  - **FIT**: “Fit in existing nodes” (uses existing nodal positions).
  - **FITL** / **FITL** (“Linear Fit in existing Nodes…”): linear interpolation of geometry into existing nodal data.

  The default is not a fixed numeric value (shown as “!”), meaning **NO must be explicitly provided** either as an element number or an option keyword.

- **NA** (unit: “–”, default: “!”)  
  **Start node** index for the cable element generation/definition. Must be provided when defining actual connectivity.

- **NE** (unit: “–”, default: “!”)  
  **End node** index.

- **NCS** (unit: “–”, default: **1.0**)  
  **Cross section number**. This selects the cross-sectional definition from elsewhere (e.g., a section library). If not specified, cross section number defaults to **1**.

- **PRE** (unit: **[kN]**, default: **0.0**)  
  **Prestress force** applied to the cable. The provided context clarifies that this prestress is considered **as geometric stiffness** in linear-elastic analyses (and is active in all load cases), and therefore requires special handling regarding load superposition.

- **GAP** (unit: **[m]**, default: **0.0**)  
  “gap of contact”. This indicates an initial clearance relevant to non-linear contact/tension behavior. From the context: features like GAP/CRAC/YIEL are intended for **non-linear analysis**, so the user must ensure the chosen analysis program version supports these capabilities.

- **CRAC** (unit: **[kN]**, default: “–”)  
  **Tensile rupture force** threshold. It is typically meaningful only in non-linear/tension-only behavior (per the context note about when GAP, CRAC, YIEL become effective).

- **YIEL** (unit: **[kN]**, default: “–”)  
  **Yield force** threshold. Also generally relevant only for non-linear behavior, depending on supported material/nonlinear formulations.

### Optional subdivision items

- **DIV** (unit: “–”, default: “–”)  
  Defines **subdivision in elements**: how many segments the cable should be divided into, which affects discretization and nodal distribution along the cable.

- **NM** (unit: “–”, default: “–”)  
  Optional **third subdivision node** parameter. The context points to comments in the **NODE** record section for interpretation details. It allows additional control over where subdivision nodes are placed.

### Contextual interpretation (from the provided notes)
Cable elements in **linear-elastic analysis behave like truss elements** (tension and compression), while **non-linear procedures** must be used for cable-sag or tension-only behavior. The table therefore includes additional parameters (GAP, CRAC, YIEL) that are only activated in non-linear analyses. Prestress (**PRE**) is always applied (active in all load cases), and thus cannot generally be combined via simple load superposition using program MAXIMA; it is often better modeled as a load. The **PROP** keyword in **NO** allows setting default property values (e.g., setting **NCS** for subsequent CABL records).

The table describes the **BEAM** input record used to define a 2-node beam element with an associated cross-section definition (typically via **BSEC**) and various options controlling discretization, hinges, orientation, buckling/span coefficients, and eccentricities.

At the start, **NO** is the element number or a literal option (type **- / LIT**). **NA** and **NE** specify the **start** and **end** beam node numbers, respectively; these are mandatory to define the beam’s connectivity in the global model. **NCS** identifies the **cross section** used for the element. It can be a single section number or two section numbers (e.g., start/end variation). The default shown is **1**.

**DIV** controls **equal partitioning** of the beam along its length (i.e., element subdivision count). In combination with mesh directives (described in the context text), DIV determines how many beam elements are generated for a given BEAM definition. **NM** is an optional third subdivision node (ref. **NODE** record), enabling non-uniform partitioning based on an additional point.

Hinge behavior is controlled by **AHIN** (beam start) and **EHIN** (beam end). Each accepts either a literal hinge condition (**LIT**, corresponding to combinations such as unconstrained shear forces/moments: e.g., **N VY VZ MT MY MZ MB**, with default “no hinges”) or a reference to an **implicit hinge working law**. The context explains that hinges trigger **static condensation at element level (Guyan Reduction)**. It also notes a modeling pitfall for eigenvalue/buckling analysis: if a hinged beam is effectively transformed to a truss-like behavior, bending stiffness may be lost, so buckling could no longer be represented unless the full DOF structure is preserved via duplicate nodes, kinematic constraints, and spring elements.

**NP** defines a special beam bedding/reference-axis case: if **NP = -1**, a **reference axis beam** is generated with the beam axis aligned to the origin of the section coordinate system. If **NP > 0**, a pile/reference-axis beam element is generated with attributes taken from profile **BORE NP**.

For stability/buckling-related formulations, **BETY** and **BETZ** provide buckling length coefficients (default: **BETY = 0** and **BETZ default = BETY**). **ALFY** and **ALFZ** provide span length coefficients, with **ALFZ defaulting to ALFY**.

Local orientation is handled by **KR** and a direction vector. **KR** selects the orientation method (**LIT/-**), defaulting to **0**. **DRX**, **DRY**, and **DRZ** define a **direction vector** (defaulted with “*”, meaning values are dependent on model/orientation choice). **DROT** adds an additional rotation about the beam axis in **degrees** (default **0**).

Finally, the table specifies beam eccentricities using **XA, YA, ZA** (start eccentricity) and **XE, YE, ZE** (end eccentricity). Values are given in **meters** (unit **[m]1001**), defaulting to **0**. **YA/ZA** are expressed in global coordinates or relative to the start/end nodes, as indicated by the descriptions:
- **XA**: eccentricity of start of beam,
- **YA, ZA**: start eccentricity in global coordinates / referenced to start node,
- **XE**: eccentricity of end of beam,
- **YE, ZE**: end eccentricity in global coordinates / referenced to end node.

Overall, this BEAM table serves as a comprehensive specification for geometry (nodes, eccentricities), section assignment (NCS/BSEC context), discretization (DIV/NM), mechanical boundary behavior (AHIN/EHIN), and specialized stability and orientation parameters (BET*, ALF*, KR/DR*, DROT).

The table defines how to specify **beam section properties along the beam axis** for a structural analysis/model. It consists of items (parameter names) and corresponding descriptions, units, and default values. The overall intent is to allow the modeler to define where a cross-section applies on a beam and to provide optional modifiers that control how these sections are interpreted, printed, and linked to beam geometry and support conditions.

### 1) Spatial position and section identification
- **X (Section location)**:  
  - **Unit:** meters (m) with a reference scale suffix shown as *[m]1001*.  
  - **Default:** marked as “!” (indicating required/critical input).  
  - **Meaning:** The coordinate along the beam where the section definition becomes effective. X is measured from a **specified reference point**. By convention it is positive toward the **middle of the beam**; **negative X values represent cantilevers**.  
  - **Additional role:** The chosen reference point also affects the **smoothing algorithm of forces at supports**.  
  - **Fallback behavior:** If options **A** or **E** are not specified, the program interprets X values relative to the **start node** of the beam.

- **NCS (Cross section number)**:  
  - **Unit:** dash (categorical identifier).  
  - **Default:** “*” (meaning typically mandatory or “use according to defined section”).  
  - **Meaning:** Selects the **cross-section type/ID** that will be used at the given location X.

- **NO (Beam number)**:  
  - **Unit:** dash.  
  - **Default:** “*”.  
  - **Meaning:** Identifies the beam to which this section definition belongs. This enables defining sections for an already existing beam. The additional context notes that continuous beams’ section blocks should follow immediately without using “NO”/predefined values—however, **with an explicit beam number**, sections may be defined for a beam that already exists.

### 2) Section special options (SPEC)
- **SPEC (Special options of section)**:  
  - **Default:** “*” (options are probably optional but impactful when used).  
  - **Meaning:** A grouped set of flags/choices that modify how the X coordinate is interpreted and how special modeling behaviors apply.

  Sub-options listed include:
  - **N:** Print the section only if explicitly requested.
  - **D:** Do not apply self-weight for this section/location (self-weight omission).
  - **A / E:** Interpret the X coordinate relative to **start** (A) or **end** (E) of the beam.
  - **S:** Interpret X as a **fraction of effective beam length**.
  - **I:** Interpolate section properties between definitions.
  - **V:** Virtual section (has infinite stiffness), used to represent rigid behavior at that location.
  - **B:** Section of bending member (bending behavior reference).
  - **C:** Section of compression member (compression reference).

These options complement the general modeling philosophy described in the additional text: internal section forces are typically “only possible for sections,” especially for non-linear analysis, and the user must define a sufficient number of sections. The SPEC options provide practical control over how many definitions are needed and how they behave.

### 3) Section type for different structural effects (beam bending/shear contexts)
- **TYPM (Type of section for main bending)**:  
  - **Default:** “LIT”.  
  - **Meaning:** Specifies what kind of section definition applies to **main bending**.
- **TYPT (Type of section for transverse bending)**:  
  - **Default:** “LIT”.  
  - **Meaning:** Specifies what kind of section definition applies to **transverse bending**.

Both TYPM and TYPT list possible values, with **SECT** indicating a regular section. Other special types represent effects at specific boundary/support faces:
- **FACE:** Face of a clamped support.
- **HFAC:** Face of a support with an articulated connection (e.g., masonry).
- **IFAC:** Section at the face of an indirect support.
- **SHEA:** Critical section for shear design.

### Overall behavioral notes from the accompanying context
The additional text emphasizes that finite element discretization can be done with constant sections per small elements, or by defining additional sections within larger beam elements; the better approach depends on the beam element implementation. For haunched beams, inclination of the centerline and variation of stiffness between sections must be accounted for. The table parameters directly support these needs by controlling:
- **where sections are located (X)**,
- **which cross-section properties apply (NCS)**,
- **how special modeling/interpretation should occur (SPEC)**,
- **how section types map to bending/shear effects (TYPM/TYPT)**,
- and **how these definitions attach to beams or continuous beam sequences (NO guidance).**

### Element identification and connectivity
- **NO**: element number or mesh option. **Default: “*!”** indicates it is mandatory. If the element number is not specified, the next free number within the current group is chosen, and duplicates are not allowed.
- **N1–N4**: node numbers defining the element corners. For **re-entrant corners** and correct **node numbering order**, the program validates geometry.  
- The table implies edge subdivision options exist elsewhere (e.g., “subdivison of edge N1–N2, N3–N4” etc.), but in this section the core connectivity is N1–N4.

### Materials and reinforcement
- **MNO**: material number for the element. **Default: \*** (uses a program/import default).
- **MRF**: material number for reinforcements. **Default: \***.

### Stiffness formulation (action selection)
- **NRA**: selects the **element stiffness formulation / element actions**. **Default: 7** (as listed in the context). The context explains that multiple actions can be combined by adding values (typically meaningful for 3D systems):
  - **0** geometry only  
  - **1** plate action  
  - **2** membrane action  
  - **4** in-plane rotation  
  Negative or combined choices are treated according to the implementation.

### Element position relative to nodes
- **POSI**: controls **element position w.r.t. the nodes**, with default **CENT**. Options:
  - **CENT** element centred at nodes  
  - **ABOV** element above the nodes  
  - **BELO** element below the nodes  
  The accompanying text notes that **BELO** can model **eccentric plates** (e.g., T‑beam effects for joists), but analysis may be restricted (requires specific system setup such as SYST SPAC in ASE).

### Thickness (isotropic and nodal/orthotropic variants)
- **T**: uniform thickness **t** of the element. Unit **[mm]** with default **1010: \***.  
- **T1–T4**: thickness at nodes K1–K4. Units **[mm]1010** with defaults shown as **T** for each node, meaning that if T is provided, nodal thickness inherits it unless overridden.
- A key note in the context: **orthotropic thickness** can’t be specified simultaneously with nodal thickness variation **T1–T4** via the orthotropy inputs **TX–TD**. Variable nodal thickness is therefore mutually exclusive with orthotropic definitions.

### Foundation bedding
- **C**: bedding coefficient **perpendicular** to element. Unit **[kN/m³]1097**, default **−1**. Context: negative values represent a **factor** relative to a BMAT foundation coefficient record; positive values specify an **absolute** coefficient.
- **CT**: bedding coefficient **tangential within the surface**. Unit **[kN/m³]1097**, default **−1**, with the same factor/absolute interpretation.

- **KR**: description of **orientation of local coordinates**; default **\*** (not fixed numerically; it indicates that KR is required or uses an import default). The context lists supported targets such as:

  - **XY/YZ/ZX** and **YX/ZY/XZ**: local x toward positive/negative global projected directions
  - **LOCX/LOCY**: toward an explicit direction
  - **nodenumber** option: align local x towards a node

- **DRX/DRY/DRZ**: direction specifications (axes direction options); units are not given in the table excerpt and default is “−”.

### Orthotropic thickness inputs
- **TX, TY, TXY, TD**: define orthotropic effective thicknesses in the local x-direction, y-direction, for lateral bending, and for torsion respectively.
  - Units: **[mm]1010**
  - Default: “−” (only active when specified).

### Table: QUAD element / mesh input parameters (continuation)

This table describes the specification options for **QUAD elements** used in surface/plate-type finite element modeling, including **edge subdivision**, **element numbering**, **action selection**, and **automatic mesh generation** with structured or interpolated geometry. The parameters also influence element orientation, eccentric placement relative to nodes, orthotropic thickness handling, and foundation coefficient scaling.

#### Edge subdivision and node connectivity
- The table specifies that edges are subdivided in two possible patterns:  
  - **Subdivision of edge N1–N2 and N3–N4** (a split corresponding to opposite edges).  
  - **Subdivision of edge N2–N3 and N4–N1** (the alternate opposite edges).  
  These subdivisions control how the surface is discretized and how many internal subareas may be generated.

#### Element number rules
- The **element number is arbitrary** if not explicitly given; otherwise the program selects the **next free number within the current group**.
- **Duplicate element numbers are forbidden**.

#### Geometry validation constraints
- The program checks **node numbering order** and detects **re-entrant corners**.
- As a general guideline, **side ratio smaller than 1:5 is not recommended**, likely to avoid distorted elements and poor numerical behavior.

#### Element actions via NRA
- Several plate/membrane/rotation behaviors can be activated simultaneously by using **NRA**.
- The **combined action** is the sum of selected values:
  - **0 = geometry only**
  - **1 = plate action**
  - **2 = membrane action**
  - **4 = in-plane rotation**
- The input is especially sensible for **3D systems** when multiple actions are combined.

#### Foundation coefficient scaling via C / CT
- Negative input values for **C or CT** do not directly assign coefficients; instead they represent a **factor** applied to the foundation coefficient from the **BMAT** record.
- Positive values assign an **absolute foundation coefficient for the element**.

#### Local coordinate system orientation (KR and DROT)
- Local axis orientation is important for result interpretation at nodes.
- KR supports reference orientation definitions including:
  - **POSX/POSY/POSZ** or **NEGX/NEGY/NEGZ**: local x aligned with positive/negative global axes.
  - **XY/YZ/ZX**: local x aligned with positive global projected directions.
  - **YX/ZY/XZ**: local x aligned with negative global projected directions.
  - **LOCX/LOCY**: local axis aligned in an explicit direction.
  - **nodenumber align local x towards a node**.
- **DROT** applies an **angle in degrees**, rotating the default coordinate system about the **local z-axis**.

#### Eccentric placement (POSI=BELO)
- If **POSI = BELO**, the element is arranged **eccentrically below nodes**.
- This is used for **plates with joists**, enabling **T-beam-like behavior** for elements with different thicknesses.
- Because eccentric plates create axial-force coupling, analysis is restricted: **only possible with SYST SPAC in ASE** (per the text).

#### Orthotropic thickness / alternative stiffness definition
- Orthotropic thickness is specified as **effective thickness in each direction**; the **normal and bending stiffness** are computed from these.
- Alternatively, a **negative section number** can be used: the section’s **area and inertia Iy** are normalized to **1 m width** and used directly as plate stiffness.
- Limitation: **variable thickness at nodes (T1–T4)** cannot be combined with **orthotropy (TX–TD)** simultaneously.

#### Structured block meshes, curved edges (M, N, COON interpolation)
- The table allows generating an **M×N structured block mesh** with curved edges and variant thickness using **Coons interpolation** between edges.
- Thickness variants can be produced by interpolation; for each edge:
  - **Positive mid-node number** ⇒ quadratic (isoparametric) interpolation
  - **Negative value** ⇒ circular geometry
  - **Zero** ⇒ straight edge
- Generated nodal coordinates are compared with existing nodes; new nodes are created only if needed.

#### Triangle meshes and diagonal control (:T1/:T2)
- If a literal **“:T”** is appended, a **pure triangular mesh** can be created.
- The QUAD elements are divided along the **short diagonal**:
  - **:T1** or **:T2** determines whether the first or second diagonal is used.

#### Mesh generation methods: KMSH, IMSH, COON/structured options
- **KMSH** is described as a GENF-derived method but not fully aligned with newer SOFIMSHA concepts.
- When only **three nodes N1–N3** are given, the method:
  1. subdivides/collects nodes along that edge,
  2. copies those edges in parallel along the remaining edge to form an **irregular but structured mesh**,
  3. keeps node numbering fully structured.
- The “variant with free node numbers” would require additional **TRAN** commands before FIT can be used.

#### Default property propagation (PROP)
- Using **QUAD PROP** with NO sets **default values** (e.g., thickness T and material MNO) for subsequent QUAD records and imports.
- Any later thickness definition **resets defaults** for orthotropic thickness behavior.
- Example intent shown:
  - Setting **T and MNO** in PROP makes them defaults for following QUAD elements.
  - Later records can re-enable orthotropy by specifying **TX, TY, TXY, TD**.

#### Import-source property preset
- When a QUAD record specifies an element number **after PROP at item N1**, the properties can be **preset from the current IMPO (import) database** for that element.

#### QUAD FIT and subdivision rules
- **QUAD FIT** creates QUAD elements even if edge subdivisions differ, by adding up to **six internal quadrilateral subareas**.
- Conditions:
  - For quadrilateral parts, the **number of odd subdivisions must be even** (allowed: 0/2/4).
  - For triangular areas, the **triangular inequality** must hold for any permutation (a+b ≥ c).
- Pure triangle meshes require **QUAD MESH** with explicit division **N**.

#### QUAD FITS on existing regular structures
- **Surface meshes on existing regular BRIC structures** can be generated with **QUAD FITS**, reserved for special cases.

### Practical usage
Use **M12/M23/M34/M41** when you want to define a structured QUAD with **curved or higher-order edges** on one or more sides. Provide only the sides that require mid-side definition; other edges can remain defined purely by their corner node endpoints.

The table defines the input data fields of the **BOUN boundary element** (a foundation/support representation with elastic bedding, typically based on the **Winkler assumption**). It is used to describe boundary elements such as **post-processing or elastic support conditions** for structural lines; a boundary element record is started with a boundary element designation (**TITL**) and then followed by any number of segment-definition records. In general, **the first node number of a new segment record must equal the last node number of the previous record**, ensuring continuous coverage of the boundary along the selected structural line.

### Field-by-field meaning (columns: Item, Description, Unit, Default)

- **NA** (Start node or element number)  
  Unit: — (nodal identifier)  
  Default: “!” (mandatory)  
  Sets the beginning of a boundary segment; used together with **NE** to define the span.

- **NE** (End node number)  
  Unit: —  
  Default: “!” (mandatory)  
  Sets the end of the boundary segment, defining the interval [NA…NE] over which the intermediate nodes are selected/covered.

- **NIV** (Increment of numbers or literal sequence selector)  
  Unit: `- /LIT`  
  Default: `*`  
  Controls how intermediate nodes between NA and NE are selected:  
  - numeric increment (e.g., take every NIV-th node), or  
  - literal **FIT** / **FITL** to use a nodal sequence (NODE).  
  The asterisk default indicates “use as-is / not fixed”.

- **TYPE** (Direction of support)  
  Unit: `LIT`  
  Default: `!` (mandatory)  
  Specifies which degrees of freedom receive elastic support. Options include:
  - **CX, CY, CZ**: translations in global X/Y/Z  
  - **CN**: longitudinal direction  
  - **CT**: both transverse directions  
  - **DX, DY, DZ**: rotations about global axes  
  - **DN**: rotation about longitudinal direction  
  - **DT**: rotations about both transverse directions  
  - **MNNN**: material number for SBFEМ  
  This controls whether the support acts in one direction (e.g., “N” plus RX/RY/RZ) or in both transverse directions (T).

- **CA** (Bedding constants at the beginning)  
  Unit: `[*]*`  
  Default: `!` (mandatory)  
  Elastic foundation stiffness parameter(s) at NA. Bedding constants may vary linearly/depending on REF (if CA ≠ CE).

- **CE** (Bedding constants at the end)  
  Unit: `[*]*`  
  Default: `CA`  
  Elastic foundation stiffness parameter(s) at NE. If not specified, it defaults to CA (constant bedding along the segment).

- **REF** (Axis for the increase if CA ≠ CE)  
  Unit: `LIT`  
  Default: `*`  
  Determines where the interpolation from CA to CE is applied when they differ:  
  - `XX`: global X-axis  
  - `YY`: global Y-axis  
  - `ZZ`: global Z-axis  
  Default `*` means use the default behavior (typically interpolation along real length per documentation).

- **RX, RY, RZ** (Support direction definition N in global coordinates)  
  Unit: —  
  Default: `*` (automatic/unspecified meaning)  
  Used to define the desired support direction when the direction is not uniquely determined in 3D by T. These values define direction **N** based on global components and the direction differs between nodes. RX/RY/RZ are used to constrain elastic support in only one perpendicular direction if desired.

- **DIV** (Equal partitioning of edge segment)  
  Unit: —  
  Default: `-`  
  Legacy/optional parameter to create intermediate nodes by equal subdivision at segment ends (not used in the presented excerpt for defaults).

- **PROG** (Geometric progressions of created nodes)  
  Unit: —  
  Default: `-`  
  Optional parameter to place created intermediate nodes with geometric spacing.

- **TITL** (Boundary element designation)  
  Unit: `LIT24`  
  Default: —  
  Record label/title (boundary element name) used to describe the boundary element. It is part of the header concept: a boundary element consists of an initial record allowing input only for **NA (= element number NO)** and **TITL**, followed by segment records describing intermediate parts.

**Contextual modeling implication:** The BOUN element represents a **continuous elastic foundation** via a spring matrix, which behaves like linearly interpolated displacement compatibility between nodes. It is compatible with QUAD/BRIC-style elements and supports selection of stiffness directions via TYPE and (if needed) RX/RY/RZ, enabling realistic foundation support along boundary regions while respecting FE partitioning (foundation reactions mainly act at the nodes).
